::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Complete [Diblock copolymer](diblock-copolymer.qmd). We keep its two connected
Gaussian polymers and change only their scattering weights.
:::

A normalized form factor starts at one. That helps us compare curve shapes,
but hides the overall scattering strength. Let's see the difference using
just **two subunits connected end to end**:

```text
blockA.end1 ~~~~ blockA.end2 = blockB.end1 ~~~~ blockB.end2
```

## 1. Build the diblock

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb

world = pyseb.World("DiblockNormalization")
graph = world.Add("GaussianPolymer", "blockA")
world.Link("GaussianPolymer", "blockB.end1", "blockA.end2")
world.Add(graph, "diblock")

parameters = {
    "Rg_blockA": 3.0,
    "beta_blockA": 1.0,
    "Rg_blockB": 5.0,
    "beta_blockB": 1.0,
}
q = np.geomspace(0.001, 2.0, 200)
```

Lengths are in nm and q in nm⁻¹. `beta` is a subunit's total **excess
scattering length**, relative to the solvent. Here we use arbitrary but
consistent scattering-length units.

## 2. Ask for both kinds of curve

Use the same structure and parameters with two different methods:

```{python}
normalized = world.EvaluateFormFactor("diblock", parameters, q.tolist())
scattering = world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized("diblock", parameters, q.tolist())
```

| Method | What it returns | Value at q = 0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EvaluateFormFactor` | Normalized form factor, F(q) | 1, when total beta is nonzero |
| `EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized` | Single-particle scattering, including its strength | Total beta squared |

Both blocks have beta = 1, so total beta is 2. The unnormalized curve starts
at **4**, while the normalized curve starts at **1**. They are related by

$$
I_{\mathrm{single}}(q)=(\beta_A+\beta_B)^2F(q).
$$

SEB calls the normalized quantity **F(q)**. Other sources often call it
**P(q)**, so always check the definition of “form factor”.

## 3. Change the weights, keeping the same geometry

First, double the scattering length of **both** blocks:

```{python}
both_doubled = dict(parameters, beta_blockA=2.0, beta_blockB=2.0)
doubled_normalized = world.EvaluateFormFactor("diblock", both_doubled, q.tolist())
doubled_scattering = world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized("diblock", both_doubled, q.tolist())
```

Then make block B invisible by matching its contrast to the solvent:

```{python}
only_A = dict(parameters, beta_blockB=0.0)
only_A_normalized = world.EvaluateFormFactor("diblock", only_A, q.tolist())
only_A_scattering = world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized("diblock", only_A, q.tolist())
```

The block is still part of the model. Its zero excess scattering length
means it makes no contribution to the scattering.

## 4. Compare the curves

The left panel divides each curve by its own forward value. The right panel
retains the scattering strength. Both panels use the same three cases:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the same diblock with and without normalization"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharex=True)

axes[0].loglog(q, normalized, label="Both blocks: beta = 1")
axes[0].loglog(q, doubled_normalized, "--", label="Both blocks: beta = 2")
axes[0].loglog(q, only_A_normalized, label="Only block A visible")
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"$q$ [nm$^{-1}$]", ylabel="Normalized F(q)", title="Compare shapes")
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].loglog(q, scattering, label="Both blocks: beta = 1")
axes[1].loglog(q, doubled_scattering, "--", label="Both blocks: beta = 2")
axes[1].loglog(q, only_A_scattering, label="Only block A visible")
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$q$ [nm$^{-1}$]", ylabel="Single-particle scattering", title="Keep the scattering strength")
axes[1].legend()

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

| Case | Total beta | Normalized F(0) | Unnormalized scattering at q = 0 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Both blocks have beta = 1 | 2 | 1 | 4 |
| Both blocks have beta = 2 | 4 | 1 | 16 |
| Only block A is visible | 1 | 1 | 1 |

**Doubling both weights leaves the normalized curve unchanged.** Their
relative weights are the same, while the unnormalized scattering increases
fourfold.

**Hiding block B changes the normalized curve too.** Scattering now sees only
block A rather than the whole diblock. Normalization removes the overall
strength, not the relative weights or interference of the visible parts.

A curve that falls faster after normalization therefore does not necessarily
represent less scattering. Each curve has been divided by a different
forward value.

## 5. From one particle to a measurement

The unnormalized result is single-particle scattering, not yet the intensity
of a solution. For dilute, independent identical particles,

$$
I(q)=n I_{\mathrm{single}}(q)+B,
$$

where n is particle number density and B is background. Absolute intensity
also requires consistent units. Here the unnormalized curves are in the
squared scattering-length units chosen for beta.

If positive and negative contrasts cancel so **total beta is zero**, dividing
by beta squared is undefined. Use `EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized`; scattering
can still be nonzero at finite q.
